c.tagline: Sahelian river capital of music, markets, and the mighty Niger.

taxi.fareNote: Fares are negotiated before the ride, not metered; shared green taxis follow set routes while 'taxi déplacement' can be chartered privately for a higher fixed price.

emergency.note: Fire brigade: 18. Response times can be slow; the U.S. Embassy recommends Clinique Pasteur or Clinique Farako for serious medical issues. Mali is under a Level 4 (Do Not Travel) advisory due to terrorism, kidnapping, and crime.

hood_landmark.Quartier du Fleuve: Palais de la Culture Amadou Hampâté Bâ, Bamako

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against all travel to Mali; avoid any travel beyond the city limits and steer clear of government, military and crowd-gathering sites where attacks and protests occur.
Armed robbery and carjacking rise sharply after dark — avoid nighttime movement, use vetted drivers, and stay away from demonstrations.

hood_desc: Bamako's modern business and diplomatic quarter, with wide paved avenues, embassies, banks, and the city's newest hotels and restaurants; suits business travelers and those wanting reliable amenities.
Central, leafy, and relatively walkable, home to the racecourse, UN offices, and a concentration of restaurants and bars popular with expats and NGO workers; a good all-round base.

A quieter university-district neighborhood on the Niger River's south bank, linked to downtown by the Pont des Martyrs; long the go-to base for backpackers and overlanders thanks to budget guesthouses.
The historic riverside core of the city, with government buildings, the Palais de la Culture, the National Museum, and the city's oldest grand hotels; central for sightseeing on foot or by taxi.
A commercial, artisan-market riverside area on the road toward Koulikoro, near Point G hill; less polished but atmospheric, with a couple of long-standing riverside hotels.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

sys.n: STUB (Société des Transports Urbains de Bamako)

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or a fare collector aboard the minibus; there is no electronic ticketing system. SOTRAMA fares are very low (roughly 25-50 cents) and set per route segment rather than metered.
transit.hours: Roughly 6am-9pm; service thins out after dark and there is little to no formal night transit, so taxis are used after dark.
transit.note: SOTRAMA green-and-yellow minibuses are the backbone of transit, supplemented by shared and private taxis; STUB buses run a smaller formal network.

train: Bamako-Kayes line (freight, very limited/irregular passenger service)
bus: intercity coaches (Bani Transport, Somatra Sarl, Binke Transport) to regional cities
ferry: Seasonal pirogue and ferry crossings of the Niger River

tip.r: Not traditionally expected; rounding up or a small tip (5-10%) is appreciated at upscale restaurants and hotels but not required elsewhere.

food.name: Tigadèguèna (groundnut stew)
food.desc: Mali's best-loved sauce: groundnut paste cooked down with tomato, onion and chilli around beef or chicken, poured over rice.

places.name: Au Bord de l'Eau
places.note: Riverside restaurant serving Malian home cooking; one of the easiest places for visitors to try it.

places.name: Bamako Kitchen
places.note: Local kitchen doing the standard Malian repertoire at everyday prices.

places.name: Marché de Medina Coura cookshops
places.note: Market gargotes ladle it out at lunchtime for a couple of thousand CFA.

food.name: Capitaine grillé
food.desc: Whole Nile perch straight from the Niger, rubbed with spices and grilled or fried, served with rice, attieke or fried plantain.

places.name: Quartier du Fleuve riverside grills
places.note: Simple riverfront tables grilling the morning's catch; point at the fish you want.

places.name: Au Bord de l'Eau
places.note: Waterfront setting with grilled capitaine as the signature plate.

places.name: Badalabougou riverbank eateries
places.note: Cluster of fish shacks on the south bank, busiest at sunset.

food.name: Riz au gras (zamè)
food.desc: One-pot rice simmered in an oily tomato and onion sauce with meat or fish and soft vegetables - the standard West African lunch plate.

places.name: Marché de Medina Coura
places.note: Women cook it in huge pots from mid-morning; one of the cheapest hot meals in the city.

places.name: Bamako Kitchen
places.note: Sit-down version of the classic street lunch, with cold drinks.

places.name: Marché de Sogoniko food stalls
places.note: Busy south-bank market with rows of cookshops serving rice plates until early afternoon.

food.name: Tô with sauce gombo
food.desc: Stiff millet or maize paste eaten by hand with a slippery okra, baobab-leaf or peanut sauce - the everyday staple of rural Mali.

places.name: Marché de Medina Coura cookshops
places.note: Around a dollar a plate; the most authentic place to eat it in the capital.

places.name: Marché de Sogoniko food stalls
places.note: Evening stalls serve tô with okra or leaf sauces to market traders.

places.name: Au Bord de l'Eau
places.note: Restaurant version if you would rather sit down by the river than eat at a market bench.

food.name: Fonio
food.desc: Tiny Sahelian grain steamed light and fluffy, served under peanut or vegetable sauce or fried as fonio djouka with onion.

places.name: Au Bord de l'Eau
places.note: Serves fonio alongside rice as the base for Malian sauces.

places.name: Bamako Kitchen
places.note: Local restaurant where fonio appears as a lighter alternative to rice.

places.name: Grand Marché (Marché Rose) food stalls
places.note: Nearby cookshops and grain sellers; also the place to buy fonio to take home.

food.name: Brochettes & dibi
food.desc: Skewers of mutton or beef and slabs of grilled sheep dusted with chilli-onion spice, wrapped in paper with raw onion and mustard.

places.name: Hippodrome street grills
places.note: Charcoal grills fire up along the nightlife strip after dark; eat standing with bread.

places.name: Marché de Medina Coura
places.note: Midday brochettes over charcoal beside the market stalls.

places.name: Sogoniko roadside dibiteries
places.note: Roadside grill shacks on the south bank doing whole-sheep dibi to order.

food.name: Bissap & ginger juice
food.desc: Deep red hibiscus infusion sweetened and chilled, and fiery fresh ginger juice - sold frozen in knotted plastic bags on every street.

places.name: Marché de Medina Coura vendors
places.note: Women sell bissap, ginger and baobab juice in iced bags for small change.

places.name: Amandine
places.note: Well-known patisserie and cafe with bottled local juices in air-conditioned comfort.

places.name: Au Bord de l'Eau
places.note: Fresh bissap and ginger by the glass with a river view.

food.name: Attaya (Malian green tea)
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea boiled with sugar and mint and poured from a height, served in three rounds that get sweeter each time.

places.name: Hippodrome street corners
places.note: Small charcoal braziers set up on the pavement; sitting down to three glasses is the point.

places.name: Grand Marché (Marché Rose)
places.note: Tea makers work between the stalls all day; a glass costs almost nothing.

places.name: Marché de Sogoniko
places.note: Traders brew attaya through the afternoon; easy to be invited to join.

landmarks: Grand Mosque of Bamako
A striking Sudano-Sahelian style mosque with distinctive earthen-colored minarets that dominates the Bamako skyline and serves as the city's spiritual heart.
Pont des Martyrs (Martyrs' Bridge)
The iconic bridge spanning the Niger River, connecting Bamako's two banks and offering sweeping views of river life and the bustling capital.
BCEAO Tower
A sleek modern skyscraper housing the regional central bank that has become a recognizable symbol of Bamako's contemporary skyline.
National Museum of Mali
One of West Africa's premier museums, showcasing Mali's rich archaeological artifacts, textiles, and masks in beautifully landscaped grounds.
Grand Marché de Bamako
A vibrant, chaotic maze of stalls selling textiles, spices, and crafts that captures the sensory energy and everyday commerce of the capital.
Monument de l'Indépendance
A prominent roundabout monument commemorating Mali's independence, a popular photo stop and symbol of national pride in the city center.
Bamako Cathedral (Cathédrale Sainte-Trinité)
An elegant Catholic cathedral whose twin towers and colonial-era architecture make it a distinctive landmark amid Bamako's bustling streets.
Point G Hill
A rocky hill overlooking Bamako offering panoramic sunset views across the Niger River valley and the sprawling city below.
Muso Kunda Museum
A museum dedicated to celebrating Malian women's history and culture, offering insight into local traditions rarely highlighted elsewhere.
Niger River Fishing Villages
Riverside communities along the Niger where wooden pirogues, fishermen, and daily river life offer an authentic glimpse of Bamako beyond the city center.

train.note: The international Dakar-Bamako train has been closed to passengers since 2010. A domestic Bamako-Kayes service was renovated and reopened in 2023 but runs irregularly with tickets sold only at the station and no online booking - do not count on it.

intl.to: Dakar (Senegal), Abidjan (Cote d'Ivoire), Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso), Conakry (Guinea) & beyond

bus.note: Regional coaches leave Bamako's Sogoniko and other gares routieres. Carry your passport for ECOWAS border crossings. Northern and central Mali have serious security risks - stick to the southern/western routes toward Senegal, Cote d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso.

ferry.note: Mali is landlocked - no international ferries. A seasonal Niger River passenger boat (COMANAV) runs Koulikoro (near Bamako) to Mopti and Gao only at high water, roughly August-December, and is domestic and irregular.

half.name: Siby
half.blurb: A village south of Bamako known for the natural sandstone Kamandjan Arch and nearby cliffs popular with hikers and rock climbers.

full.name: Kangaba
full.blurb: A town on the Niger River housing the Kamablon, a sacred thatched-roof shrine tied to the founding constitution of the 13th-century Mali Empire.
